deep.reconstruction:
PURPOSE. Gauss is fixing the epochs needed for reducing star places (aberration and nutation, as on the next page) in Göttingen sidereal time for 1801 and 1819–1821. Two quantities are needed for each year: (a) the instant of the 'astronomical beginning of the year', the moment when the Sun's mean longitude L = 280°, and (b) the mean longitude of the lunar ascending node ☊ at that instant. The base data are taken from Burckhardt's lunar tables (1812).

1) Sun's mean motion in 100 Julian years (36525 days) = 36000°45'52.7" = 129 602 752.7".

2) Motion of the lunar node in 100 Julian years = 1934°10'12" = 6 963 012.0" (retrograde).

3) [implicit, mine] Tropical year Y = 36525·1296000/129602752.7 /100 = 365.24224227 days. Gauss writes this further down as '1 Sonnenjahr = 365,24224227 Tage'.

4) Node motion per tropical year = 69630.12"·Y/365.25 = 69628.641" = 19°20'28.641". Gauss corrected 'Jahre' to 'Sonnen J[ahr]'.

5) Period of the node = 1296000/69628.641 = 18.6130302 tropical years. In Julian years it would be 18.61263, so the unit must be 'Sonnenjahre'.

6) Epoch 1801 Jan 0, 12h Paris mean time: L☉ = 280°9'13.8", ☊ = 13°54'58.7".
- With the Sun's daily motion 3548.33"/d, L reaches 280°0'0" earlier by 553.8/3548.33 ≈ 0.15607 d.
- So the astronomical beginning of 1801 is Jan 0.3439194 (Paris mean time).
- The node, moving 190.637"/d retrograde, is then larger by about 29.75": ☊ = 13°55'28.453".

7) Sidereal time at that instant: 1216972, i.e. 0.1216972 d = 0.3439194 − 2/9.
- Reason [mine]: when the mean Sun's longitude is 280°, its right ascension is 18h40m.
- The sidereal time then equals 18h40m + mean solar time, i.e. mean time − 5h20m.
- 5h20m = 2/9 day.

8) Paris–Göttingen longitude difference = +0.0211343 d (30m26.0s) 'in G'.
- Göttingen sidereal time of the L = 280° instant: 0.1216972 + 0.0211343 = 0.1428315. This is the column 'Anfang des J. *2', 1801 Jan 0.1428315.

9) Gauss's remark: this applies if the year begins when the Sun's mean longitude is 280°, but 'in der Tafel' a moment 5h20m of sidereal time later is the basis. So the tabular beginning of the year, in Göttingen sidereal time, is 0.1428315 + 0.2222222 = 0.3650537. Numerically this equals the Göttingen mean time of the L = 280° instant.

10) Later years, adding the tropical year (fraction 0.24224227) and dropping whole calendar days:
- 1819: 0.3650537 + 18·0.24224227 − 4 = 0.7254146
- 1820: +0.2422423 gives 0.9676568
- 1821: +0.2422423 − 1 (1820 is a leap year) gives 0.2098991
- The *2 (L = 280°) value for 1821 is 0.2098991 − 2/9 + 1 = 0.9876769 (Jan 0, i.e. it falls on the previous day).

11) Node at the tabular instant, 5h20m sidereal = 0.2216155 mean days later:
- Correction −0.2216155·190.6369" = −42.248".
- 1801: 13°55'28.453" − 42.248" = 13°54'46.205".
- 1820: subtract 19 years' motion (19·69628.641") modulo 360°, giving 6°25'42.026".
- 1821: subtract a further 19°20'28.641", giving 347°5'13.385".
- The 1819 entry is left blank; it would be 25°46'10.667".

12) Final note: this same instant is labelled differently in different works.
- In the present astronomical book it is dated −1 January.
- In the Danish tables (probably Schumacher's) it is dated +1 January.
- In special tables for (probably) a circumpolar star of Ursa Minor it is dated 0 January.

The values feed the next page: aberration constants a, b, c, the Burckhardt node table, and arguments counted from 1819 Jan 1, 0h Göttingen sidereal time.
errors: Slight internal inconsistency in step 6, about 0.6 s. With the Sun's daily motion 3548.33"/d and L = 280°9'13.8" at Jan 0.5, the start comes out 0.3439266, not 0.3439194 (difference 7e-6 d). The node value 28.453" fits either to within 0.002". This is negligible and possibly due to the reading of the Sun's seconds.

No arithmetic errors were found in the year-start chain (1801 → 1819 → 1820 → 1821), the 2/9-day sidereal shift, the longitude addition, or the node values for 1801, 1820 and 1821. All reproduce to the last digit.
Gauss's own correction 'Jahre' → 'Sonnen J' is necessary: the period 18.61303 and the motion 19°20'28.641" are per tropical year, not per Julian year.

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine practical-astronomy computations: epochs and node arguments for star reduction from Burckhardt's tables. Gauss's use of the L = 280° (fictitious-year) convention around 1818–19 sits alongside Bessel's contemporaneous practice, and the note explicitly compares the conventions of existing tables. There is no new mathematics.

checkable.asserts: sidereal time at the L=280° instant = 0.1216972 (mean time minus 5h20m)

transcription_corrections: 'Jul. Jahre' after 18,61303029 should be 'Sonn[en] Jahre' (tropical years); the value only fits tropical years.
'⊙ = 280.0.9.13.8' should read 280° 9' 13.8" (implied by the 0.156-day offset and the node shift).
'1216972 St. Z.' means 0,1216972 in sidereal time; '+0,0211743[?] in G' should be +0,0211343 in Göttingen (longitude Paris→Göttingen).
In the final list, 1801 is 0,3650537, not 0,3650337 (needed for 1819 = 0,7254146).
The year column under 'Anfang des J.' reads 1801, 1819 (overwritten), 1820, 1821, 1822; the 9876769 entry belongs to 1821.
Node column: '347. 4[?] 13. 385' should be 347° 5' 13.385"; the three node values belong to 1801, 1820 and 1821, with 1819 blank.
'd'Urnae' is probably 'd. Ursae [minoris]' (special tables for a pole star); 'astr. Buche' is uncertain.
